metaDescription: Six 80 amp automatic transfer switches for generators and solar backup compared by phase, poles and voltage protection, with permit and electrician notes.
expertTake: The GEYA GPS8-17 80 amp single-phase switch is the best overall pick because it combines fast transfer, a live voltage display and an adjustable priority source in one module. The VORTULIUK 2-pole unit is the plain alternative for single-phase generator and solar backup. Anyone who needs a UL-listed residential transfer switch with an outdoor cabinet should skip this class of dual-power modules and ask an electrician for a listed switch instead.
introParagraphs: Switches rated near this size mostly come in a different form from the cabinet kits people picture. They are compact dual-power modules that watch two sources and flip a contactor between them, often used with a generator, a battery inverter or a solar setup.

That makes the buying questions different too. Phase, pole count, voltage protection and what the module does when power returns matter more than breaker counts, and the question of listings and inspection becomes a front-line issue rather than a footnote.

products.name: GEYA GPS8-17 80A 110V automatic transfer switch

specList.label: Priority
specList.value: Adjustable L1 or L2 preferred source

products.description:
The GPS8-17 monitors two power sources and switches to the backup within 0.2 seconds if the primary fails. A built-in LED display shows live voltage, and the module protects against over-voltage and under-voltage conditions before it commits to a source.

The feature that sets it apart is the priority selector. You can designate source one or source two as the preferred supply, so when the favored source returns, the switch moves back automatically. That is useful when the grid is the preference, and equally when a solar and battery system should be the first choice.

Compared with the VORTULIUK, you get the display and the priority logic, which make setup and troubleshooting easier. A module like this still needs a licensed electrician, a proper enclosure and a permit, and it should be matched to the generator's voltage and frequency. Because the display shows real voltage, it is also a handy diagnostic when a portable generator runs rough: you can see sag under load and decide whether to shed circuits. Owners should mount the module in a ventilated, dry enclosure, label both sources clearly and keep a printed copy of the setup values inside the door.
products.bestFor: Single-phase generator or solar backup where a readout helps.
cons: Module format needs a separate enclosure
Listing marks need confirming for inspection

products.name: PJERJZN 80A 110V automatic transfer switch, auto and manual
products.description:
This switch is marketed for American homes, with a 110 volt, 80 amp rating and a choice between automatic and manual operation. The listing highlights over-voltage and under-voltage protection, and it gives you the option of hands-free switching or a manual setting.

The manual mode is the quiet advantage: if you do not trust automatic behavior with a certain generator, you can run the switch by hand and still have a physical isolation device. Next to the GEYA, it gives up the display and the priority selector, and it asks you to rely on indicators and the manual.

As with all of these modules, confirm what enclosure it needs and what listing marks it carries. A licensed electrician and a local permit are required, and the generator's voltage must be stable before the switch will accept it. A cheap generator with a wandering output can leave an automatic switch waiting, so run the generator for a minute and watch the indicators before concluding anything is faulty. If you travel, have a neighbor or family member know where the manual setting is and how to use it.
products.bestFor: Households that want automatic switching with a manual fallback.
cons: No live display on the module

products.name: VORTULIUK 2-pole 80A 110V PC-class dual power switch
products.description:
VORTULIUK labels this a PC-class, professional-grade dual power module intended for single-phase generators and solar systems. It has auto and manual modes, indicator lights for each source and built-in voltage protection, and it works with 50 or 60 hertz dual-supply systems.

The PC-class designation means it is built for infrequent switching, which is exactly the generator use case. The green indicator tells you when the primary source is healthy, and the manual mode lets you take control. Against the GEYA, there is no readout, but the two-pole layout is a clean match for a simple single-phase load.

Check the enclosure, wire gauge and breaker upstream with your electrician, and obtain a permit. Make sure the solar or inverter source is compatible with a switch that does not parallel sources. Grid-tied inverters shut down when the grid drops, so the switch and inverter must agree on what happens during an outage. Ask the installer to explain the sequence in plain words and write it down for the household.
products.bestFor: Single-phase generator or solar changeover without extras.

products.name: Fafeicy 4-pole 80A dual power automatic transfer switch
products.description:
Fafeicy builds this module as a compact four-pole switch with millisecond-level switching and a flame-retardant polycarbonate housing. The listing describes it as a dual power source arrangement where one source is common and the other is the backup.

Four poles switch the neutral along with the lines, which can matter in installations where the neutral must be handled by the transfer device. That is a point to discuss with the electrician rather than assume. Compared with the VORTULIUK 2-pole, you get a fuller switching arrangement at the cost of a bulkier module.

Because the description is short on electrical detail, have the installer verify voltage, frequency and wiring before purchase. A permit and a licensed electrician are required. Neutral switching is the detail most worth settling early, because it changes how the generator is bonded and how the panel is arranged. A short design sketch from the installer before purchase can prevent a swap later.
products.bestFor: Compact installations where the neutral is switched.
pros: Four poles switch the neutral as well
cons: Sparse electrical detail in the listing

products.name: GEYA GPS8-18 80A 3-phase automatic transfer switch
products.description:
The GPS8-18 is the three-phase sibling of the GPS8-17. It watches all three phases of both sources and switches to backup automatically, with protection for over-voltage, under-voltage and overcurrent and adjustable trip points.

The priority selector lets you choose which phase acts as the preferred source for the automatic return. That is a tool for a workshop, a small commercial site or a farm with three-phase equipment, not for a typical house.

Because it is a three-phase device, installation and commissioning should be handled by a qualified electrician who understands the supply. Permit rules apply, and the generator must provide matching three-phase output. A phase-loss event is a real concern for motors, so the protection settings are worth reviewing with the installer rather than leaving on factory defaults. Document the trip points you choose and keep the record with the equipment.
products.bestFor: Small commercial or farm sites with three-phase supply.
pros: Over, under voltage and overcurrent protection
cons: Not suited to typical single-phase houses

products.name: VORTULIUK 4-pole 80A 3-phase dual power switch
products.description:
This four-pole VORTULIUK module monitors the main source continuously and transfers to the backup if it fails. The listing describes automatic and manual modes and a built-in voltage protection that cuts out unsafe supply levels on 110 volt systems.

It is a plainer three-phase option than the GEYA GPS8-18, with fewer adjustable settings and no display noted in the listing. The four-pole layout switches the neutral, and the PC-class label points to infrequent switching.

Use a licensed electrician to specify the enclosure, wiring and protection, and expect a permit. Treat the listing as a starting point and request the full manual before ordering. Where the GPS8-18 lets you tune trip points, this unit leans on built-in thresholds, so confirm that those thresholds suit your motors. If the seller cannot supply a wiring diagram, treat that as a reason to look elsewhere.
cons: No display mentioned in the listing

buyingCriteria.explanation: The GPS8-17, PJERJZN and the 2-pole VORTULIUK suit single-phase homes, while the GPS8-18 and the 4-pole VORTULIUK are three-phase. Most houses are single-phase, so buying a three-phase module is a common error. Check your supply before ordering. The label on the meter or panel, or a quick look at the service drop, tells the electrician in seconds, and it avoids a return after the box has been opened.

The 2-pole VORTULIUK switches the two lines, while the Fafeicy and the 4-pole VORTULIUK also switch the neutral. Whether the neutral should be switched depends on how the generator is bonded. Ask the electrician rather than guessing. A wrong choice can leave a neutral tied to ground in two places, which creates stray current and a shock hazard.

The GPS8-17 shows live voltage and protects against over and under voltage. Others rely on indicator lights. A display makes it easier to see why a transfer did or did not happen. Without one, a blinking light and a manual are all you have when the generator is running and the house is still dark.

Most of these modules are sold without a cabinet. A bare module needs an enclosure, and the unit's own listing marks may not match what a residential inspector expects. Treat the inspector's view as part of the purchase. A quick call to the building department before ordering can save a rejected installation, and it is worth asking what marks they require on dual-power equipment.

The PJERJZN and both VORTULIUK units offer manual as well as automatic modes. A manual fallback is useful when a generator's output is unsteady. It also lets you test without waiting for an outage, which is when you most want to know the switch works.

An 80 amp switch ties into the service or a sub-panel and needs a licensed electrician and a local permit. Do not wire it yourself. A miswired transfer device can backfeed the grid or damage equipment, and a lineman restoring power in your street is the one who pays for it.

specDecoder.meaning: A dual power rating for infrequent switching, as in standby use. It is not built for frequent daily transfers, so it suits a generator that runs a few times a year but not a setup that cycles sources constantly.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Fafeicy and both VORTULIUK units use it.

specDecoder.meaning: The number of poles switched. Four poles include the neutral.
How quickly the module moves to the backup after the primary fails. The figure describes the contactor, not the whole system, since the generator still needs time to start and settle.
A setting that picks which source is preferred when both are healthy. It decides which supply carries the load when utility power returns.
The module refuses an unsafe supply level and waits for a stable one.
specDecoder.watchFor: The PJERJZN and the VORTULIUK units list it.

howWeEvaluated.title: Phase and poles
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each module to single-phase or three-phase use and noted the pole count. The GPS8-18 and the 4-pole VORTULIUK are three-phase. The 2-pole VORTULIUK is single-phase. Picking the wrong phase is the most common way to end up with a module that cannot be used, so this was the first filter before any feature comparison.

howWeEvaluated.title: Protection
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for voltage and overcurrent protection. The GPS8-18 adds overcurrent trip settings. Listings with no protection details scored lower, since a transfer device that accepts any voltage can pass a bad supply to the house. Voltage windows matter most with portable generators, whose output can swing under changing load.

howWeEvaluated.title: Setup and visibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed displays, indicators and priority selectors. The GPS8-17 leads with a live readout. Simple indicator lights scored as adequate. Visibility matters because the person using the system during an outage is often not the person who installed it.

howWeEvaluated.title: Listing clarity
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked how clearly each listing states ratings and modes. Sparse listings such as the Fafeicy scored lower. A manual and wiring diagram matter at this size.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered enclosure needs, switching class and inspection risk. Findings rely on spec sheets and owner feedback patterns, not lab work. These are modules, so installers matter.

cards.label: Two-pole
cards.text: The VORTULIUK 2-pole and the GEYA GPS8-17 switch the lines only. They are simple and suit many single-phase installations.

cards.label: Four-pole
cards.text: The Fafeicy and the 4-pole VORTULIUK also switch the neutral, which some generator and service arrangements require.

howToChoose.note: Let the electrician decide from the bonding plan rather than choosing by habit. A short design conversation before you order is cheap, and a wrong pole count is expensive to fix once the module is wired.

howToChoose.subheading: For Solar and Battery Pairing Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A module that states solar or inverter use, offers a preferred source setting and does not parallel sources.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The VORTULIUK 2-pole names generator and solar use, and the GPS8-17 lets you set the preferred source.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want a manual fallback and household framing, which points to the PJERJZN, or settings for three-phase loads, which points to the GPS8-18.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your setup is simple single-phase. The GPS8-17 or the 2-pole VORTULIUK covers it.

maintenance.why: Moving the switch confirms the mechanism still operates. It also checks that the indicator lights respond.
Loose terminals overheat at 80 amps. An electrician should check them with the right tool, and look for browning on the insulation, which is the first sign of a poor connection under load.
Dust and moisture damage a module. Keep the cabinet sealed, and make sure it has a drip-safe place to sit so condensation never runs onto the contactor.
A supervised run confirms the voltage and frequency match. Do it before an outage, and note the readings so you have a baseline to compare against when something seems off.
A labeled diagram helps any future electrician. Store a copy near the panel.

faq.q: Is an 80 amp module a normal home transfer switch?
faq.a: Not usually. Residential kits come as cabinets with breakers, while these are dual-power modules that need an enclosure and a careful installer. If you want a listed cabinet kit, look at the 30 amp and 50 amp guides on this site first.
Most houses are single-phase. Choose three-phase only if your service and generator are three-phase. A shop or farm with large motors is the usual place to find three-phase supply.
Four-pole units switch the neutral as well. Whether that is needed depends on how the generator is bonded.
No. A licensed electrician should install it under a permit. Miswiring can backfeed the grid.

Listings vary and often say little. Check the unit and ask your inspector before you buy. A product page that mentions a standard is not the same as a mark on the label, and the inspector reads the label.

faq.q: Can I use one with solar?
faq.a: Some listings name solar use, but compatibility depends on the inverter and the setup. Confirm with the installer. Grid-tied inverters in particular behave differently during an outage, so the sequence must be planned in advance.
